body: Shapiro, Lionel, Beall, Jc, in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry "Curry’s Paradox" says: "“Curry’s paradox”, as the term is used by philosophers today, refers to a wide variety of paradoxes of self-reference or circularity that trace their modern ancestry to Curry (1942b) and Löb (1955). [ 1 ] The common characteristic of these so-called Curry paradoxes is the way they exploit a notion of implication, entailment, or consequence, either in the form of a connective or in the form of a predicate. Curry’s paradox arises in a number of different domains. Like Russell’s paradox , it can take the form of a paradox of set theory or the theory of properties. But it can also take the form of a semantic paradox, closely akin to the Liar paradox . Curry’s paradox differs from both Russell’s paradox and the Liar paradox in that it doesn’t essentially involve the notion of negation.
